system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-05-11 17:07:00 to 2179-05-17 15:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for IV diuresis prior to a scheduled right heart catheterization to assess pulmonary artery pressures for liver transplant eligibility. He had recently completed treatment for Acinetobacter bacteremia, which led to removal of his tunneled catheter and placement of a PICC. During this admission, he received IV furosemide for fluid overload, underwent a therapeutic paracentesis removing 1.25 liters of ascites, and had a new tunneled catheter successfully placed. Right heart catheterization showed borderline normal pulmonary pressures with slight improvement, confirming no contraindication to transplant. His diarrhea, attributed to Remodulin, remained stable. He was discharged home with instructions to restart home diuretics, continue all transplant-related medications, and follow up with the liver team for ongoing management.
problems: Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Other vasodilators causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History of HCV cirrhosis complicated by diuretic-refractory
ascites, varices, hepatic encephalopathy, portal pulmonary hypertension. 
Please evaluate given low-grade fevers and increased abdominal pain and
distention.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained through the abdomen before and after the
administration of IV contrast per the CTA liver protocol.  Multiplanar
reformatted images in coronal and sagittal axes were generated and reviewed.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen from ___.

FINDINGS:  

There is an 8 mm nodule at the base of the left lung (series 3A, image 11),
not seen on the prior exam.  Note is again made of a calcified granuloma at
the base of the left lung.  There is a second nodular opacity within the
lingula which likely represents a focus of atelectasis, but also was not well
seen on the prior exam.

The patient's liver is again cirrhotic with sequela of portal hypertension
including splenomegaly measuring up to 23 cm.  There is 10 mm arterially
enhancing focus in segment VI (series 3A, image 51), not demonstrating
washout, however, not previously seen on the prior exam.  There is also a 6 mm
hypodensity without arterial enhancement, too small to characterize, however,
new compared to the prior exam.  Note is made of varices including esophageal
varices and a splenorenal shunt.  There is diffuse small-to-moderate
non-hemorrhagic ascites.

Aside from significant splenic enlargement, the spleen demonstrates multiple
granulomatous calcifications.

At the superior pole of the right kidney, there is a hyperdense lesion
measuring 2.6 cm x 2.7 cm.  The kidneys bilaterally are otherwise
unremarkable.  There is no evidence of hydronephrosis.  The pancreas is normal
without evidence of focal lesions or peripancreatic stranding.

The stomach, duodenum and small bowel are normal without evidence of wall
thickening or obstruction.  Small-to-moderate amount of ascites can be seen
tracking into the pelvis.  Prominent enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes are seen
measuring up to 2 cm.  There is no intra-abdominal free air.

CT PELVIS:  The urinary bladder is normal.  The prostate and seminal vesicles
are normal.  There is no pelvic wall or inguinal lymphadenopathy.  The colon
is unremarkable.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  No lytic or blastic lesions concerning for malignancy are
identified.  No new compression fractures are identified.  Compression
deformities, some treated, and hardware at L5-S1 are similar to the prior
exam.

IMPRESSION:

1.  10 mm enhancing lesion in hepatic segment VII and hypodense lesion in
segment V/VI without arterial enhancement appear new compared to the prior
exam.

2.  Hyperdense lesion at the superior pole of the right kidney is similar in
size compared to the prior exam, however, an ultrasound or MR is recommended
for further evaluation.

3.  Nodular opacities at the base of the left lung may be secondary to
atelectasis, however, appear new compared to the prior exam.

4.  No rim-enhancing fluid collection to suggest abscess is identified.

5.  Cirrhosis with sequelae of portal hypertension including splenomegaly and
varices including esophageal varices and splenorenal shunt are overall stable
compared to the prior exam.

Close attention on follow up imaging is recommended.

HISTORY:  ___ male with cirrhosis now with fevers.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph dated ___.  

FINDINGS:

Portable semi erect chest radiograph demonstrates low lung volumes with
subsequent bronchovascular crowding and atelectasis.  There is bibasilar
atelectasis with no definite focal consolidation identified.  Enlargement of
the central vessels with mild vascular congestion is identified.  No overt
pulmonary edema.  Heart size is top-normal.  There is a enteric tube which
descends in an uncomplicated course its terminal end out of view.  A right
central line is seen with its tip terminating in the low superior vena cava. 
There is no appreciable pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  

IMPRESSION:
No pneumonia.

INDICATION:  HCV cirrhosis with low-grade fevers, malaise and abdominal pain. 
Evaluate for SBP.

PRE-PROCEDURE IMAGING AND FINDINGS:  There is a small amount of ascites seen
in all four quadrants.  The largest fluid pocket, in the left lower quadrant,
was targeted for paracentesis.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (radiology attending) and Dr. ___
(radiology resident).

PROCEDURE:  The procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives were discussed
with the patient and written informed consent was obtained.  A preprocedure
timeout was performed, discussing the planned procedure, confirming the
patient's identity with three patient identifiers and reviewing a checklist
per ___ protocol.  Under ultrasound guidance, an entrance site was selected
and the skin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. 
Approximately 10 mL of 1% lidocaine was instilled for local anesthesia. 
Subsequently, a ___ ___ catheter was advanced into the largest fluid
pocket in the left lower quadrant and 2 liters of red colored fluid was
removed.  A portion of the ascites was sent for analysis including
microbiology, cell count and chemistry.  A single ___ Vicryl stitch was placed
for hemostasis.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complications. 
Estimated blood loss was less than 5 mL.

Dr. ___ radiologist, was present throughout critical portions of
the procedure.

IMPRESSION:  Ultrasound-guided therapeutic and diagnostic paracentesis with
removal of 2 liters of reddish-colored fluid.  Laboratory analysis is pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand you've been feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had a headache, stomachache, and no appetite for a couple days. I had a low fever yesterday—around 100.3. I get those sometimes with infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chills, cough, or sore throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chills or cough. But I do feel short of breath and my sinuses are congested. My belly feels more swollen than usual too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned you were with your niece who was sick—any chance you caught something from her?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She had cold symptoms, so maybe. But I’m worried—my tunneled line has caused infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that carefully. We’re going to run blood tests, a urine test, and possibly a paracentesis to make sure there’s no infection in your ascites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just feel so tired and achy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on you. Your vitals are stable—temperature is normal now, heart rate and oxygen levels are okay on your usual 4 liters of oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood and urine cultures came back with no growth so far. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So it’s not a blood infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from what we see so far. But we’ll keep monitoring. We’re also going to do a CT scan to check your liver and lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Your liver looks stable with cirrhosis and varices, but we see a couple of new small spots—one in the liver and one in the lung. Nothing looks like an abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they cancerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Too early to say. They could be benign. We’ll follow up with your liver team. Nothing urgent, but we’ll keep an eye on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are negative. No sign of bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I still feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your chest X-ray shows some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—but no pneumonia. We think you have a viral upper respiratory infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just a cold?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. We’ll treat your symptoms. We’re also going to do a paracentesis today to check your ascites fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just removed 2 liters of fluid from your abdomen. It was reddish, but that’s not uncommon. We’ll test it to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help? My belly still feels full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help over the next few hours. We’ll keep monitoring your comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fluid analysis shows a white blood cell count slightly elevated but no bacteria seen. Culture is negative. So no sign of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not an infection in the belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We think your symptoms are from the viral URI. We’ll give you a nasal spray—fluticasone—to help with congestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep Ativan available for nausea. It should improve as you start feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still tired, but the congestion is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your CMV and EBV tests came back negative. No other viruses detected. We’re confident it’s a mild viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver and transplant status?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MELD labs are stable. You’re still on the transplant list. The portopulmonary hypertension is stable on your current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking better. Your breathing is easier, and your exam shows less abdominal tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. But I’ve been gaining weight—worried it’s more fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition saw you. They think you might be getting too many calories from the tube feeds. They recommend reducing from 18 to 16 hours a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So cut back on the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same rate, just shorter time. We’ll monitor your weight daily. Call if it goes up more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative. You’re improving steadily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed pain meds much. And no nausea since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if you keep this up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the nasal spray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with fluticasone—use it twice daily for congestion. Continue all your regular meds, including rifaximin, nadolol, and Remodulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Reduce to 16 hours a day. Follow up with the liver clinic as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spots on the CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver and kidney findings need follow-up imaging. Your liver team will arrange that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t another serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you dodged that. Keep using the nasal spray, watch your weight, and call if you develop fever or worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with low-grade fever, malaise, and increased abdominal distension. He had recently been exposed to a family member with cold symptoms. Workup included negative blood, urine, and ascites cultures, ruling out bacteremia and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Imaging showed stable cirrhosis and new but non-urgent findings in the liver and lung. His symptoms were attributed to a viral upper respiratory infection, which improved with supportive care including fluticasone. A therapeutic paracentesis removed 2 liters of fluid. Nutrition recommended reducing tube feeding duration from 18 to 16 hours daily due to suspected caloric excess. He remained stable on his transplant regimen, including Remodulin for portopulmonary hypertension. He was discharged home with improved symptoms and follow-up planned with his liver team.
